No.11

How to Prevent Hidden Depression Among Those Around Us?

A record of inspired teaching on hidden pain and companionship, with a reading note on mental-health crisis.

Author's record · translated; the Chinese original is authoritative

Open in reading mode →

🔶Inquiry to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva

I asked the Bodhisattva: many people with depression show nothing on the outside. Someone may be cheerful and positive in the morning and gone by the afternoon. How can we prevent this when someone is at immediate risk of suicide?

🔶The Bodhisattva's Teaching

Some smile in the light of day,
yet are wounded in the night.
It is not that they are fickle;
it is that their suffering is deep.
The one truly in danger
is not the one who grieves, but the one who grows "still".
When someone suddenly no longer argues,
no longer pours out their pain,
no longer asks for help,
but becomes strangely calm,
let all beings know —
that is not letting go;
the heart of parting has already arisen.

To save a person is not a matter of many words,
but of "not leaving".
When there is one who is willing to stay beside them,
the gate of hell is already half closed.
Do not ask why they want to die;
first ask them:
"May I stay with you?"

You ask about those weighed down by sorrow, who smile in the morning light and take their lives at dusk; such a suffering heart is beyond what eyes can see and words can reach.

The thoughts of beings rise like a sudden wind; once the thought of death arises, it is like fire burning within a house — nothing shows outside, yet within it is already charred.

To prevent it, do not only watch the face; observe whether the heart has lost its strength. What can save them is but three things: first, accompany their heart, so they are not alone; second, protect their surroundings, lessening what presses upon them; third, receive their wishes, and lead even one thought toward life.

Yet if the winds of their karma are fierce and their will already set, even when others do all they can, sometimes they cannot be kept.

Then do not blame yourself; help with what comes after, so that their consciousness does not fall into terror. Sorrow is not powerlessness; sorrow is the peace that follows having done all you could."

🔶Plain Rendering

Some people can still smile during the day, yet suffer alone at night. This is not because their moods change easily, but because the pain inside is too deep to show. The person in immediate danger is often not the one crying and grieving, but the one who "suddenly goes quiet". When someone stops arguing, stops complaining, even stops asking for help, and instead becomes unusually calm, those around them should be alert — this may not be "having let go", but being ready to leave. Helping such a person does not take many reasons or arguments; it only takes "not leaving". As long as one person truly stays with them, they can be pulled halfway back from the abyss of despair and pain. Do not rush to ask "why do you want to die?" First let them know: "Can I stay by your side?"

You ask about people in extreme inner pain who still smile in the morning yet may end their lives by evening — this kind of deep suffering often cannot be seen from the outside, nor fully put into words.

A person's thoughts rise suddenly like the wind; once the thought of death arises, it is as if the inside of a house is already being consumed by fire while the outside shows no trace.

To prevent this, you cannot only look at appearances; you should notice whether their heart has become completely exhausted.

There are only three things that can help: First, keep their heart company, so they do not feel alone; second, protect their environment, reducing the pressures that push them; third, take in their wishes and guide them to hold on to at least a thread of the thought "I want to live".

However, if the other person's karma (or psychological storm) is too fierce and they are set on dying, sometimes even those who do everything they can cannot keep them.

At such a time you should not blame yourself, but help with what comes after, so that their consciousness does not fall into greater fear and pain.

True compassion is not blaming yourself for being powerless; it is, after doing all you can, letting the heart come to rest in peace.
